items.title: Dolly Parton Essentials
items.description: Dolly Parton (1946-2026) was one of the most popular and highly respected singers and songwriters in the history of Country music. She rose from a humble background to become not only an iconic music star but also a successful business entrepreneur. She is one of the most honored artists of all time, with a record breaking number of hit songs and countless awards. Dolly Parton passed away on August 25, 2026. She was 80 years old. (Photo: Rovi)

items.title: Tracks & Traces: Dolly Parton
items.description: With Tracks & Traces, we aim to expand the horizon around a given artist with related tracks and similar artists in order to present a deeper insight into their music. Dolly Parton has been a significant music force ever since she broke through the charts in the late 1960s. With her recognisable voice, gifted songwriter skills and strong identity she paved way for female singers in many genres over the years, and her journey from poverty to massive crossover success has served as inspiration to numerous artists. Parton moves flawlessly from bluegrass to countrypolitan, from pop bangers to Christian hymns, and thus is she one of the most influential artists of our time. This playlist tracks down some her musical roots - and follow just a couple of the many influences by her. (Photo: Rovi)

items.title: Covering Dolly Parton
items.description: Dolly Parton (1946 - 2026) will forever be ranked as one of the major American songwriters. She penned around 3000 songs through a career that lasted seven decades, inspiring countless artists across styles and genres. Here are just some of the finest Dolly Parton cover songs recorded. (Photo: Rovi)

items.description: Dolly Parton released "Jolene" 	October 15, 1973, as the first single and title track from her album of the same name. items.title: Pop for Beginners
items.description: New to Pop? These carefully-selected 25 tracks will serve as your beginner's guide to some of the best the genre has to offer. Use them as a jumping-off point to discover even more great Pop. From foundational hitmakers to modern day bops, these tracks will help paint the overall picture. Press play and let the learning commence!

items.title: Classical for Beginners
items.description: New to classical? These carefully-selected 20 tracks will serve as your guide to some of the best the genre has to offer. Use them as a jumping-off point to discover even more great classical music. From the 1600s through to the twentieth century; from orchestral works to famous opera arias to chamber music gems; this playlist introduces you to some of the most important composers of Western classical music from Europe and the United States. You'll immediately recognize the famous four-note motive at the beginning of Beethoven's Fifth, and the prelude to Bach's First Cello Suite, performed here by renowned cellist Yo-Yo Ma, is an instant ear-worm. Some of these tracks you may never have heard before, but are incredibly influential: Igor Stravinsky's "Rite of Spring" set off a riot when it was first performed, and the descending bass line from "When I Am Laid In Earth" by Henry Purcell can be found in modern music across all genres. Consider this your first class in classical music history.

items.title: Jazz for Beginners
items.description: New to jazz? These carefully selected tracks will serve as your beginner's guide to some of the best the genre has to offer. Jazz's century-plus history is impossible to encapsulate in 20 recordings, but few could argue with the sheer artistic brilliance of these tracks. Consider this your era-spanning, cross-stylistic crash course in America's most gorgeous art form.

items.title: Indie for Beginners
items.description: New to indie rock? These carefully selected 20 tracks will serve as your beginner's guide to some of the best the genre has to offer. Use them as a jumping-off point to discover even more great indie. /// A nebulous term and tradition, “indie” rock and pop entered the lexicon during the 1980s and gained serious traction in the ’90s, signifying “independent” guitar bands signed to labels operating outside the FM-radio mainstream. Not surprisingly, “indie” bands tended to find their stylistic roots in punk and post-punk, art pop, experimental rock and other underground sounds. As its sister term, “alternative,” came to embody unabashedly commercial-sounding radio rock in the late ’90s and aughts, “indie” became a kind of catch-all for collegey, hipster-approved music of various stripes – from driving guitar rock to dancey, atmospheric, synth-based alt-pop – regardless of its major-label affiliations.

items.title: Mafioso Rap 101
items.description: The creation of mafioso rap is attributed to Kool G Rap during the late 80s, yet it was during the mid-90s when the subgenre really took off with songs from Raekwon, JAY-Z, Nas, and more. Mafioso rap enabled artists to paint lyrical pictures of the money-making machinations that exist everywhere from gritty inner-city New York to luxurious high-rise condos. The lyrical content is the important focus, allowing producers to be more elastic with the sound, although most of it features a hard-hitting kick drum. (Photo: Rovi)

items.title: Salsa 101
items.description: Salsa is perhaps the one genre immediately associated with the American Latinx identity. And rightfully so. It was created by Cuban and boricua communities in 1960s New York City—with a hodgepodge of influences ranging from Cuban son, jazz, mambo, bomba y plena and so many more. The list of legends—Hector Lavoe, Celia Cruz, Marc Anthony, Willie Colon, Johnny Pacheco, Tito Puente, Joe Arroyo, Ruben Blades—reads like a Hall of Fame full of heavy hitters. (Cover: Celia Cruz x Marc Anthony / Rovi x Press)

items.title: Moombahton 101
items.description: Combining the DIY attitude of post-bloghouse dance music, the syncopation of reggaeton, and the decelerating properties of THC, moombahton is the hybrid genre that was never supposed to be more than an inside joke. Created in 2009 by Washington, DC-based DJ/producer Dave Nada, moombahton’s popularity spread quickly thanks to the proliferation of international DJ-headlined music festivals, where Nada and many of his friends (including Diplo and Dillon Francis) would perform year-round. It started as a genre of DJs simply slowing down existing records and soon artists were producing original tracks with the sound’s signature 100-108 BPM, a refreshing change of pace amid the frenzy of bass music and radio-oriented EDM. (Cover: Dave Nada, Dillon Francis; Photo: Rovi)

items.title: Vocal Jazz 101 (With Commentary)
items.description: Probably the best way to define genuine vocal jazz is to say that the jazz singer is just another jazz musician on the bandstand. In other words, a jazz singer has the privilege of performing with just as much studied freedom as a great instrumentalist. They can savor a melody or lyric with passion; use wordless technique to scat an improvised tune; screech and wail onto avant-garde terrain; work on the frontline, reading complex themes alongside the other “horns”; and much more. Jazz vocal groups have proven that the music’s ensemble chemistry isn’t exclusive to instruments. Singing permeates the entire history of jazz, from the blues roots of Ma Rainey and Bessie Smith, through the scat innovations of Louis Armstrong, the big-band stardom of Frank Sinatra and the utter splendor of Billie Holiday, Ella Fitzgerald and Sarah Vaughan. With a special introduction by vocalist Veronica Swift. (Cover: Billie Holiday [top], Ella Fitzgerald/Photos: William P. Gottlieb/Library of Congress)
